lead: C++ lets you define your own types — enumerations that give names to a closed set of values, and structs that bundle related data under one label. After this chapter you will be able to model a problem domain with `enum class` and `struct`, write the helper functions that operate on them, and confidently apply aggregate initialization, `const`-reference passing, and the `.` vs `->` member-access distinction.

aids.title: One-way implicit conversion: enum to int, not int to enum
aids.md: The implicit conversion for an unscoped enum runs in only one direction: an enumerator silently converts *to* an integer, so `std::cout << green` compiles and prints `1`. The reverse — assigning a raw integer *to* an enum variable — always requires an explicit cast: `Color c { static_cast<Color>(2) }`. Writing `Color c { 2 }` is ill-formed and will not compile, which is exactly the type-safety boundary the lesson is explaining.

aids.title: Declaration order is initialization order
aids.md: In aggregate initialization, values in the brace list are matched to struct members *in the order those members are declared*, not by name. If `Point` declares `x` first and `y` second, then `Point p { 1, 2 }` sets `x = 1` and `y = 2` — swapping the numbers in the braces swaps the fields, not the names. Any member that has no corresponding value in the list is value-initialized (zero for `int`).

aids.title: . for objects and references, -> for pointers
aids.md: A reference and an object use identical syntax at the call site: both use `.`. The `->` operator is *only* for pointers — `ptr->line` is shorthand for `(*ptr).line`. If you see LLVM code with `M->getOrInsertFunction()`, `M` is a pointer; if you see `I.getDebugLoc()`, `I` is an object or reference.

aids.title: Templates generate types, not instances
aids.md: `template <typename T> struct Pair` is a *pattern*, not a usable type on its own. Writing `Pair<int>` asks the compiler to stamp out a concrete `struct` where every `T` is replaced with `int`; `Pair<double>` stamps out a separate concrete struct. You must supply the type argument (or let CTAD deduce it) before you can create an object — `Pair p` with no argument is an error unless deduction is available.

xrefs.md: The `std::optional<Campaign>` return type used in the string-to-enum helper was introduced in Chapter 12 as the clean way to represent a value that may or may not exist.
Passing structs by `const T&` and mutating through `T&` applies the reference and pointer conventions established in Chapter 12.
The requirement that template definitions be visible at the point of use — placing them in headers rather than `.cpp` files — follows the same logic as function templates introduced in Chapter 11.
